scope.quote: This paper investigates the relation between accrual reliability and earnings persistence.
Our empirical tests employ a comprehensive categorization of accounting accruals in which each accrual category is rated according to its reliability.
The third major contribution of our work is to corroborate and extend Sloan’s findings regarding market efficiency with respect to information in accruals.
Our second prediction is that (g22g1) will be more negative for less reliable accruals.
The univariate regressions have two shortcomings. First, they do not allow for formal statistical tests of differences in the r2 estimates across accrual components.

review_notes: Source-first selection: the abstract and introduction identify the relation between accrual reliability and earnings persistence as the central question. The retained main model is Table 5 Panel C’s final joint OLS regression using the extended balance-sheet decomposition. The source says the univariate regressions cannot test coefficient differences; the joint specification includes all components. Table 5 Panels A/B are benchmarks and coarser preceding decompositions; the univariate rows are preliminary comparisons. Table 6’s longer horizon, Table 7’s further tests, and Table 8’s stock-return/mispricing analysis are later or downstream questions.

The source-defined operating and financing uses of “short-term investments” differ by context: current operating assets use the combined cash and short-term investments field (Compustat item 1), while financing FINA identifies short-term investments as item 193.
